title: The Pneumatic Post
subtitle: How cities once moved their mail by air pressure, and why the idea keeps returning

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the nineteenth century, the commercial districts of Europe's largest cities faced an unusual communication problem. The electric telegraph could carry a message between cities in minutes, yet once a telegram reached a central office it still had to be taken across town by messenger boys on foot or on horseback. In congested streets, this final stage of the journey could take longer than the entire long-distance transmission. The solution that engineers proposed seems, in retrospect, almost whimsical: a network of underground pipes through which small containers would be pushed or pulled by air pressure. Between the 1850s and the 1950s, systems of this kind were built in more than forty cities, from Paris and Berlin to Rio de Janeiro and New York.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle was straightforward. A cylindrical carrier, usually made of leather-covered steel and roughly the size of a rolled newspaper, was placed inside a brass tube. Steam-driven pumps at a central station then either compressed the air behind the carrier or removed the air in front of it, so that the capsule was driven forward by the difference in pressure. A single carrier could hold around thirty-five folded telegrams. The earliest London line, opened in 1853 between the Stock Exchange and the main telegraph office, was only 200 metres long, but by the 1870s Paris had built a radial network in which lines spread outwards from central exchanges to dozens of district post offices. Keiko Sato, a historian of engineering, has shown that this radial layout was the key to the network's efficiency, since a message only ever needed to pass through one central exchange rather than a chain of intermediate stations.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For several decades the system performed remarkably well. According to the transport historian Margaret Ellison, a carrier in central Paris travelled at an average of 30 kilometres per hour, which was faster than any vehicle on the streets at the time, and its speed did not depend on traffic or weather. The Parisian public adopted the service with enthusiasm. A message written on a special blue card, known as a petit bleu, could be posted at one office and delivered to an address on the other side of the city within two hours, making it, in Ellison's words, 'the e-mail of the Belle Époque'. At its peak in the 1930s, the Paris network carried more than ten million items a year through some 450 kilometres of tubes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the technology had weaknesses that became more serious as networks expanded. Carriers occasionally jammed, particularly at junctions or where tubes had been damaged by building work, and locating a blockage beneath a busy street was slow and expensive. Engineers developed an ingenious way of finding stuck carriers by firing a pistol into the tube and timing the echo, but repairs still required the road surface to be dug up. The economist Lars Hedberg, who has examined the accounts of the Berlin system, argues that its operating costs per message rose steadily after 1900, largely because the pumping stations consumed large quantities of coal and needed permanent staff. The price the public paid for each message, by contrast, was fixed by the postal authorities and barely changed for decades.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The decline of the pneumatic post was gradual rather than sudden. As the telephone spread into offices and homes in the early twentieth century, fewer people needed to send short written messages across the city. The teleprinter, which allowed telegrams to be printed directly at local offices, then removed the original reason for the tubes altogether. In some cities war hastened the process: Berlin's network was badly damaged in 1945 and later divided by the political border that ran through the city. Most systems closed between the 1950s and the 1980s. Paris, perhaps out of affection as much as necessity, kept its network running until 1984, and part of Prague's survived until floods destroyed its machinery in 2002.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pneumatic tubes did not disappear, however. They remain common in hospitals, where they carry blood samples and medicines between wards and laboratories, and in supermarkets and banks, where they move cash safely from tills to a secure office. Some commentators see the old city networks as a forerunner of more ambitious modern schemes. The engineer and writer Tomás Ribeiro points out that recent proposals for high-speed passenger capsules travelling through low-pressure tubes rely on the same basic physics as the nineteenth-century post. Ellison is more cautious. In her view, the lesson of the pneumatic post is not that the technology was flawed but that it was overtaken: a system designed to solve one specific problem could not adapt once that problem had been solved by other means.
